text: If the Pauli gates are the alphabet, the Hadamard gate is the first word that actually does something uniquely quantum: it turns a definite classical-looking state into an equal superposition. Nearly every quantum circuit you'll see from here on opens with an H gate.

The Hadamard matrix is 1 over root 2 times the matrix 1, 1, 1, negative 1. H on ket-zero gives 0.7071, 0.7071 — called the plus state. H on ket-one gives 0.7071, negative 0.7071 — the minus state. Squaring each amplitude's magnitude gives measurement probabilities of 0.5 and 0.5 for both outputs. Plus and minus aren't the same state though — they differ by exactly the kind of relative phase you saw Z produce last lesson, invisible to measurement alone.

H is its own inverse: apply it twice to ket-zero and you land back exactly on ket-zero, no rounding drift, no leftover superposition, because H squared equals the identity. That matters practically — every physical qubit starts, by convention, in ket-zero, which on its own carries no more information than a classical bit. H is the standard first move in a circuit because it's the simplest unitary that bakes genuine 50/50 measurement uncertainty into the amplitudes themselves. It's also the first half of one of the most important two-qubit constructions in the field: Chapter 3 builds the Bell state using H on one qubit followed by a CNOT with a second.

Next lesson introduces two finer-grained phase gates, S and T, which rotate an amplitude's angle without ever changing a measurement probability on their own — until Chapter 4's universal gate sets put that property to work.
